title: Two swapped cells cover each other as they pass
body:
`swap` in `crates/acre/tests/scene_examples.rs` animates a swap by keyframing each cell's `offset` track along the row. The two cells travel the same straight line in opposite directions. At the midpoint they sit on the same slot, and the cell painted later hides the other. Frame 33 of the `array_swap` example shows four cells, `2`, `1`, `4` and `3`, with `5` hidden behind `1`.

The scene model has no swap of its own, and `swap` is a helper in the test. A swap written in the language will have the same problem unless the two cells move along different paths.

## Open

- Move the cells along arcs, one above the row and one below.
- Lift the cells off the row by different amounts before they slide.
- Accept the overlap.

I lean to arcs, because they show which two cells traded places. A `Track<Point>` moves in a straight line between two keyframes, so an arc needs either many keyframes or a curved path in `Track`.

notes.author: Jack Roddy/ed2a7ee0
notes.text: Commit 456e6c9 draws a cell that is moved or scaled at an instant after the last row, above every cell that is not. A character that travels across a row, or from one row into another, now stays visible over the cells it passes. This does not fix the swap. Both cells of a swap move, so both are drawn late, and the one with the higher index still covers the other at the midpoint. The language can now write a swap as two `move ROW N DX DY` actions, so the bug reaches the language, as this issue said it would. The `swap` helper in `crates/acre/tests/scene_examples.rs` builds a `Grid`, which the commit does not touch.

notes.author: Jack Roddy/ed2a7ee0
notes.text:
Fixed in b009f84, in the `swap` helper of `crates/acre/tests/scene_examples.rs`. Jack chose the first option, arcs.

Each cell now lifts 48 px (one cell height plus 8), slides along the row, and drops, with ease-in-out on each leg. The cell at the lower column goes above the row and the other below. I used a lift, slide and drop and not a sampled arc. A cell moving along a circular arc starts to overlap its neighbour in the row after a few pixels of sideways travel, because the lift is still near zero. The lift-first path clears every cell it passes as well as the swap partner. The test asserts that the two boxes stay apart in x or y at 201 instants.

The same swap as a canvas `timeline` works today. A `row` with `move r 0 0 -48; move r 3 0 48;` then `move r 0 120 -48; move r 3 -120 48;` then `move r 0 120 0; move r 3 -120 0;` in three consecutive spans renders the same frames. Cell moves are absolute, so each leg names the full offset. Nothing is missing for this motion. A true curved path would still need many short spans, because `move` goes in a straight line between its ends.
